    How a loss becomes systemic

    A systemic event needs four things at once: an excess that can unwind, channels for the loss to spread, too little liquidity to absorb the forced selling, and a shock that actually tests the system. Each link is scored 0–100 against its own history; the index is their average. The weakest link tells you where trouble would start.

    The index through past crises

    Weekly Systemic Risk Index since 2005, with each link shown faintly behind it. Shading marks the level bands.

    Source and method. Equal-weight average of the four link scores; each indicator is ranked against its own history using only data available at the time (expanding window). Composite design follows Holló, Kremer & Lo Duca (2012, ECB CISS) and the survey in Bisias, Flood, Lo & Valavanis (2012); out-of-sample evaluation follows Giglio, Kelly & Pruitt (2016). Data: FRED, BIS via FRED, Yahoo Finance.

    Does the index work?

    A real-time test, as if the index had been run every month since 2010 using only data available then. For each month we predict the bad-case (10th percentile) outcome over the next 12 months and compare the forecast error with simply using the historical 10th percentile. A positive score means the measure beats history; Giglio, Kelly & Pruitt (2016) run the same test on 19 published systemic risk measures.

    How this monitor works

    Why four links

    The literature splits systemic risk into the build-up of vulnerabilities and their amplification once a shock hits. The Build-up link covers the first. Contagion and shock absorbers are the amplifiers: one is about who is exposed to whom, the other about whether there is cash to absorb forced selling. Trigger is the shock itself. A high reading in one link alone is rarely a crisis; 2008 had all four.

    How scores work

    Every indicator is ranked against its own history (0 = calmest week on record, 100 = most dangerous), using only data available at the time. Link scores average their scored indicators; the index averages the links. An indicator is scored only if published work shows it predicts crises and it has no known structural break in our sample; this rule was fixed before the out-of-sample test. Others are shown as context: the data is real and current, but adding it to the score would mislead, because it double counts another indicator, trends up for decades, lags the cycle, measures a global rather than US channel, or has no published evidence of predicting crises. Each context row says which. Bands are set from the index's own crisis peaks (see the ruler above).
